clue.text: Funny number?

parts.note: read 'number' as something that numbs, an anaesthetic, and 'funny' as one that makes you laugh

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a comic song or a joke routine on a variety bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a figure or a song; here it is a numb-er, a thing that deadens feeling, as the dentist's nitrous oxide does.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrous oxide is an anaesthetic gas whose nickname comes from the giggling it can provoke.

clue.text: Did he love to swim? Just the opposite!

definitions.text: Did he love to swim? Just the opposite!

parts.words: Did he love to swim? Just the opposite!
parts.note: flip the question: the Greek youth did not love swimming, he swam to reach his love each night across the Hellespont

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether some man enjoyed swimming, answered with a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek legend Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit Hero, and drowned when her guiding lamp blew out; so he swam to love rather than loved to swim.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical lover who swam the strait to his beloved Hero fits the reversed phrase exactly.

clue.text: Wise man supports university practice

indicators.note: in a down clue the wise man sits beneath the university and so holds it up

parts.note: a sage is a wise man

explanation.surface: A learned scholar backs up the way a university does things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supports' is the placing signal: in a down answer the piece for 'Wise man' goes below U.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is customary practice, the habitual way something is done.

clue.text: Rough-made organisation of wartime volunteers

indicators.note: an organisation of the letters is an arrangement of them, so the letters of the words before are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A hastily assembled body of citizen soldiers raised during the war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organisation' reads as a body of people, but it signals rearranging the nine letters of ROUGH MADE. The Home Guard was Britain's volunteer defence force of the Second World War, often thought of as rough-and-ready.
explanation.definitionFit: The Home Guard was a force of part-time civilian volunteers who defended Britain during the Second World War.

clue.text: Very plain facial feature?

parts.note: plays on the saying 'as plain as the ___ on your face', meaning perfectly obvious

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on an unattractive part of a face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' suggests ugliness, but the clue leans on the idiom for something obvious, which names the feature in the middle of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as plain as the nose on your face' makes this feature the proverbially obvious one.

clue.text: Talk with the French politicians may be illuminating

parts.note: gas is informal for idle talk or chatter
la is the French feminine form of 'the'
MPs are Members of Parliament

explanation.surface: Chatting with French politicians could prove enlightening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Illuminating' reads as 'enlightening' about the chat, but the definition is literal: things that give light.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamps burning coal gas were the street and household lighting of the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Fire about fifty for being lax

indicators.note: the word for fire goes around, or about, the numeral

parts.note: to fire someone is to sack them
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: An employer dismisses about fifty staff for being careless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' places L inside SACK, between the A and the C.
explanation.definitionFit: Slack and lax are synonyms, both meaning careless or not strict.

clue.text: Obtains information about raising money for the future

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising means the whole construction is read upward, from bottom to top
the word for information wraps around the word for obtains

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
gets means obtains

explanation.surface: Someone gathers facts about fundraising for later on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising' turns the whole container upside down in the down entry; 'about' looks like 'concerning' but is the wrapping signal. GEN is everyday British slang for facts.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum saved up for later life.

clue.text: One involved in two matches at the same time

definitions.text: One involved in two matches at the same time

parts.words: One involved in two matches at the same time
parts.note: 'matches' reads as sporting fixtures, but here means marriages, held simultaneously

explanation.surface: A sportsperson playing in two games at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matches' suggests games; read it as marriages and the person is wed to two spouses at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone married to two spouses at the same time commits the crime of bigamy.

clue.text: Mass trial arranged for scaremongers

indicators.note: arranged signals that the letters of the two words before it are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A large-scale trial organised to deal with people spreading panic.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarmists and scaremongers both spread needless fear.

clue.text: Wrongly equated with a mile?

definitions.meaning: the proverb 'a miss is as good as a mile' equates a near miss with a big one

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is the proverb meaning a narrow failure is still a failure; split the answer as two words, A MISS.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiss means wrongly or faultily; read as a near miss, the proverb says it is as good as a mile.

clue.text: Remove the sediment from port

parts.note: 'port' suggests the wine, which is decanted off its sediment; here it is a harbour whose silt is scooped out

explanation.surface: Instructions for decanting a bottle of vintage port.
explanation.walkthrough: Vintage port throws a crust that is decanted off; but read 'port' as a harbour and the job is clearing silt from the seabed.
explanation.definitionFit: Harbours are kept navigable by scooping mud and silt from the bottom.

clue.text: One has to fire on the run in this sporting event

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the run follows the word for fire

parts.note: to fire is to sack
a race is a run

explanation.surface: An event in which someone must shoot while running, like a biathlon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' suggests shooting; it means SACK. In this school sports-day race, competitors jump along with their legs in sacks.
explanation.definitionFit: A school sports-day race in which runners hop along inside bags.

clue.text: TV programme that's being reviewed?

parts.note: 'reviewed' looks like 'critiqued', but split it as re-viewed: watched again

explanation.surface: A television show currently under critical assessment.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'reviewed' as re-viewed: a programme shown a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: A rerun is a broadcast shown again, so viewers see it a second time.

clue.text: Select shafts for soil-loosening tools

parts.note: to pick is to select
axes, plural of axis, are shafts or spindles on which things turn

explanation.surface: Choosing handles for gardening implements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shafts' looks like handles; here it means axes, the plural of axis.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickaxes are heavy pointed tools swung to break up hard ground.

clue.text: Unruly apes get the ruler for talking

indicators.note: unruly apes are disorderly, so their letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: Badly behaved monkeys get a monarch to speak for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unruly' rearranges the four-letter animal word to SPEA; 'ruler' tempts as a measuring stick but is a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking and talking are synonyms for uttering words.

clue.text: Feeling weak, but the tide is about to turn

definitions.meaning: in low spirits or poor health

definitions.text: the tide is about to turn
definitions.meaning: the literal sense: the sea at its lowest point, just before it starts to come in again

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for low spirits is also a literal description of the tide at its lowest, just before it turns.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for being in a poor state comes from the sea's lowest point, when the water is about to flow back in.

clue.text: It keeps food warm when transferring to the lap

indicators.note: transferring means the letters of the three words are shifted into new positions

explanation.surface: Dinner stays hot while being carried over to someone's knees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transferring' rearranges the eight letters of TO THE LAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A heated metal surface or plate on which dishes are kept hot before serving.

clue.text: Not the best of the entries, usually

definitions.text: Not the best of the entries, usually

parts.words: Not the best of the entries, usually
parts.note: 'entries' looks like competition submissions, but means ways into a house; the rear one is rarely the grandest

explanation.surface: A judge's verdict on a competition submission that falls short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entries' suggests contest entries; read it as entrances. The rear one is usually humbler than the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear entrance of a building is usually plainer than the front one.

clue.text: Page fasteners?

definitions.meaning: The traditional name for a pageboy, as in the pantomime Cinderella
small discs pushed through holes to close clothing

explanation.walkthrough: A pageboy in a hotel or great house was nicknamed after the rows of brass fastenings on his jacket; Buttons is the page in the British Christmas pantomime Cinderella.
explanation.definitionFit: Pageboys were called Buttons after their uniform's many brass studs, and those discs also close clothing.

clue.text: Suitable cut-out for computer

indicators.note: out means the word for cut sits outside the word for suitable

parts.note: to lop is to cut
apt means suitable

explanation.surface: A fitting cardboard shape to stand in for a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut-out' looks like one noun meaning a cardboard shape; split it so 'out' sets the word for cut around the word for suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable computer small enough to rest on the knees.

clue.text: Indicate there's some wine to finish off

parts.note: port is a fortified wine from Portugal
to end something is to finish it off

explanation.surface: Someone signals there is a little wine left to polish off.
explanation.definitionFit: To portend is to signal or foreshadow something to come.

clue.text: Strange patterns found in church

indicators.note: strange means odd, so the letters of the next word are made odd by being rearranged

explanation.surface: Peculiar designs discovered inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges PATTERNS.
explanation.definitionFit: A transept is the crosswise arm of a cross-shaped church building.

clue.text: Quiet little person wants place for books

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet
an elf is a small fairy-tale creature

explanation.surface: A tiny, hushed figure is looking for somewhere to keep the library.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookshelf is a flat board fixed to hold volumes.

clue.text: Metal washing machine?

definitions.meaning: a large boiler once used in British homes to heat water for laundry

explanation.walkthrough: In older British homes a copper was a big metal tub in which washing was boiled; the question mark flags this dated sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is a reddish metallic element, and the old laundry boiler took its name from that metal.

clue.text: It sounds like the height of resentment

indicators.note: sounds like says the word for the height is spoken and a word sounding the same is entered

parts.note: a peak is the height or summit

explanation.surface: Someone describes the very summit of bitterness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The height of resentment' reads as extreme anger; instead the summit word, said out loud, gives the French-derived word for irritation.
explanation.definitionFit: Pique is a feeling of irritation or wounded pride.

clue.text: Dust one may well find on the bathroom shelf

definitions.text: Dust one may well find on the bathroom shelf

parts.words: Dust one may well find on the bathroom shelf
parts.note: 'dust' suggests grime to be cleaned off, but here it is a powder kept there on purpose

explanation.surface: A housekeeper notes the grime that collects on a bathroom shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dust' suggests the dirt you would wipe away; it is a body powder deliberately kept in the bathroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Talcum powder is a fine mineral dust patted on the skin after bathing.

clue.text: Daisy is kind of neat to look at

parts.note: neat is an old word for cattle, so an ox
to eye something is to look at it

explanation.surface: Someone says a daisy is rather a tidy flower to view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy, but it is the archaic word for cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: The ox-eye is a large white wild daisy of meadows and verges.

clue.text: Ballet posture of Lincoln in square dance

indicators.note: in places the name for Lincoln inside the rearranged letters
dance means the letters of square jig about into a new order

parts.note: Abe is short for Abraham Lincoln, the US president

explanation.surface: Abraham Lincoln strikes a pose during a square dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dance' turns the letters of square into ARSQUE; 'square dance' looks like one folk-dance phrase, but it is fodder plus indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: An arabesque is a ballet position balanced on one leg with the other extended behind.

clue.text: Pain

parts.note: read the word not as suffering but as a word in another language, the one spoken across the Channel, naming a staple loaf

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pain' is the French word for bread, so the answer translates it rather than defining hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: In France the everyday word for a loaf is spelt p-a-i-n, so the clue word is itself the baked thing.
